title: Practical: Logger Interface
story: Your app has a bug, but only in production — where logging is turned off. You need a logging system that can write to the console during development, write to nowhere in production, and maybe write to a file someday. The Logger interface decouples 'what to log' from 'where to log it.'
why: The Logger pattern is the canonical real-world interface — it separates the logging concern from the implementation, letting you swap backends without changing a single line of application code.
analogy: The Logger interface is like a water pipe — the pipe specification (interface) defines 'water must flow through.' You can connect it to a faucet (ConsoleLogger), a drain (SilentLogger), or a storage tank (FileLogger). The house (application) doesn't care where the water goes, as long as the pipe fits.
try_it: Add a `TimestampLogger` that wraps another logger and adds a timestamp prefix to every message (use a counter as a mock timestamp). Then add a `FilteredLogger` that only logs messages containing a specific keyword. Chain them: TimestampLogger wraps ConsoleLogger — two loggers composed together!
tips: The Logger interface decouples 'what to log' from 'where to log' — change backends without touching application code
SilentLogger is a real pattern — it's the 'null object pattern,' useful for tests and production when logging is expensive
Different loggers can have different internal state — the interface only cares about the log() method
common_mistakes: Hardcoding `io.println` throughout your code instead of accepting a Logger — impossible to disable logging in production
Making the Logger interface too specific — `log_error`, `log_warning`, `log_info` are three methods; one `log(level, msg)` with a level enum is cleaner
Forgetting that the Logger is a DEPENDENCY — pass it in, don't create it inside the function
